evidence_set: Story recall on day 3 was still lower in the ketamine group: immediate 7.75 (2.08) against 10.18 (2.99), delayed 6.73 (2.55) against 9.76 (3.30) (immediate recall group × day F(1,37) = 7.55; delayed recall group and day effects without an interaction). The ketamine group's day-3 immediate recall did not differ significantly from the comparison group's first-night score, and the authors conclude that the day-3 recall differences likely reflect a lack of practice, because the drug impaired memory of the first session. Editors' observation from Table 1: the ketamine group's day-3 delayed recall (6.73) was close to the comparison group's first-night score (6.87).

Ketamine use was known only from what people said: hair samples were collected on day 3 but not analysed because the resources were not available, and drugs and amounts could not be confirmed. On the night, all 20 in the ketamine group and 17 controls had smoked cannabis, and 65% and 72% had drunk alcohol, more than 2 hours before testing; 36% of the ketamine group took more ketamine after testing but, by their own account, none on days 1 to 3; everyone reported alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1 and 2, at similar levels in the two groups, and none on day 3. University-level education: 15 of the ketamine group against 18 controls; 4 in the ketamine group and 1 control had been prescribed antidepressants in the past.

evidence_set: Three days after a night of use, the ketamine group, which reported using ketamine from twice a week (12%) to once a month (12%), rated dissociation 17.75 (17.41) against 5.37 (7.21) (p<0.008) and state schizotypal symptoms 62.35 (25.35) against 26.42 (20.45) (p<0.001), with magical ideation 28.25 against 11.00, compared with peers with little or no ketamine use, whose scores correlated highly across the two days (r = 0.93 and 0.94), although their mean schizotypal score fell from 33.37 to 26.42; both scales rate the current state. Depression on the anxiety and depression questionnaire was 4.45 (2.11) against 1.89 (1.29) on the night, a rating that covered the previous two days, and 4.30 (2.58) against 1.68 (1.29) three days later (group F(1,32) = 19.4), which the authors call low and well below the clinically significant range of 8–11.

Among 18 people who had cut down and 10 polydrug controls, state schizotypal symptoms were higher in the ketamine group at both sessions (51.5 (21.28) against 24.8 (8.16) three days after a night of use; 18.67 (17.05) against 4.0 (4.06) three to four years later; group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001) and fell in both groups; dissociation did not differ (10.11 against 5.44, then 3.24 against 0.80); at follow-up depression on the anxiety and depression questionnaire was higher (5.27 (4.32) against 2.00 (2.45); U = 55.5, P < 0.031 as printed; editors' calculation: U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives a two-tailed p of about 0.10), which the authors say was not within a clinical range; schizotypal scores did not correlate with ketamine use. Editors' note: the same page says the earlier field study's participants did not differ from controls on depression at baseline, which contradicts that paper's own report of higher depression scores in its ketamine group (Curran & Morgan, 2000, p. 585).
change: Review and adjudication, ketamine round: AI reader 232 (adjudicator) settled the second readers' findings against the PDFs. The depression clause now says what the authors call the scores (mild to moderate in Morgan et al., 2009; below clinical levels in Curran & Morgan, 2000, and Morgan et al., 2004a); the 2000 field study's ratings are named as current-state ratings, one scale built for the study; the 2004 follow-up's depression difference was measured only at follow-up and its printed test gives p of about 0.10 on recalculation; the one-year report's excess of delusional ideation in the infrequent and abstinent groups over the non-drug group, the frequent group's negative life events and the 7.08 against 11.48 discrepancy for the same session are stated. The review's statement that the one-year rise in depression was unrelated to change in use is not adopted (the primary paper does not report it).
